source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Replacing the need for responding to call lights largely, which is not the actual purpose or effect of this particular rounding protocol","B":"Applying just to clients at high fall risk, with fairly little other benefit, which understates how broadly this protocol is actually intended to help","C":"Increase nursing workload with no measurable patient benefit, similar to what the skeptical staff member is currently assuming about this protocol","D":"Proactively address needs, reducing falls and improving satisfaction, rather than simply adding busywork as the skeptical staff member assumed"}}
source_row.rationale: Structured hourly rounding protocols, in which nurses proactively check on clients at regular intervals to address common needs (pain, positioning, toileting, and ensuring personal items are within reach), have been associated in research with reduced fall rates, decreased call light use, and improved patient satisfaction, reflecting a proactive rather than purely reactive approach to care.
source_row.source_detail: Purpose and Benefits of Structured Hourly Rounding
source_row.source_name: Studer Group / AHRQ — Hourly Rounding Evidence and Implementation
source_row.stem: A nursing unit implements a structured hourly rounding protocol, in which nurses check on each client at regular intervals to proactively address common needs, and a skeptical staff member assumes this will just add busywork without actually changing outcomes like falls.
